text: pipeML provides two core workflows: compute_features.training.ML(): train tune models training set. compute_prediction(): evaluate trained models test set. already test set prepared, can also use: compute_features.ML(): one-step training + prediction.

title: pipeML
text: Load example data: example, make train/test split:
code: data = pipeML::data_example_classification X <- data %>% dplyr::select(-target) y <- data$target set.seed(123)  train_idx <- caret::createDataPartition(y, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)  X_train <- X[train_idx, ] X_test  <- X[-train_idx, ]  y_train <- y[train_idx] y_test  <- y[-train_idx]

title: pipeML
text: Train tune models using repeated stratified k-fold cross-validation: Access best-trained model: View trained tuned machine learning models: Figure 1. Models training performance.
code: res <- compute_features.training.ML(features_train = X_train,                                      target_var = y_train,                                     task_type = "classification",                                     trait.positive = "1",                                     metric = "AUROC",                                     k_folds = 2,                                     n_rep = 1,                                     file_name = "Example_classification",                                     return = F) res$Model names(res$ML_Models)

text: training, users can predict new data using compute_prediction() function. can specify metric maximize determining optimal classification threshold. Supported values maximize include: “Accuracy”, “Precision”, “Recall”, “Specificity”, “Sensitivity”, “F1”, “MCC”. Check predictions: Inspect threshold-based prediction metrics: return = TRUE, compute_prediction() saves ROC PR curves Results/ directory. Figure 2. ROC curve. Figure 3. PR curve.

title: pipeML
text: SHAP values help interpret machine learning predictions quantifying feature contributions. Visualize feature importance interactions using shapviz:
code: df = cbind(X_train, target = as.numeric(y_train)) ## compute_shap_values expects predictors and target in a single data.frame  shap_classification <- compute_shap_values(   model_trained = res$Model,    data_train = df,    task_type = "classification",    target_col = "target",    trait.positive = "2", # Notice here that because of as.numeric() our target variable changed to 1 and 2 so we will consider 2 as our new 1.   n_cores = 2,     file.name = "Example_classification" ) sv <- shapviz::shapviz(   shap = as.matrix(shap_classification$shap_values),   X = df[, setdiff(colnames(df), "target")] )  # Global feature importance (bar plot) shapviz::sv_importance(sv, kind = "bar") +   ggplot2::ggtitle("Global Feature Importance")  # Beeswarm plot shapviz::sv_importance(sv, kind = "beeswarm") +   ggplot2::ggtitle("SHAP Beeswarm Summary")  # Feature dependence plots for top 6 features top_features <- names(sort(colMeans(abs(shap_classification$shap_values)), decreasing = TRUE))[1:6]  for (f in top_features) {   print(     shapviz::sv_dependence(sv, v = f) +     ggplot2::ggtitle(paste0("Dependence: ", f))   ) }

title: pipeML
text: addition classification regression tasks, pipeML supports survival analysis, allowing users train machine learning models predict time--event outcomes. survival analysis, response variable defined two components: Time: follow-survival time Event: indicator whether event occurred (1) observation censored (0) pipeML automates training, evaluation, interpretation survival models using cross-validation SHAP-based explanations. Load example dataset survival: Similar previous example, split data train/test:
code: data = pipeML::data_example_survival X <- data %>% dplyr::select(-time, -status) time <- data$time event <- data$status set.seed(123) train_idx <- caret::createDataPartition(event, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)  X_train <- X[train_idx, ] X_test  <- X[-train_idx, ]  time_train <- time[train_idx] time_test  <- time[-train_idx]  event_train <- event[train_idx] event_test  <- event[-train_idx]

title: pipeML
text: function compute_features.training.ML() can also train survival models setting task_type = "survival". Access best model: Check training metrics: Figure 4. Models training performance.
code: res_survival <- compute_features.training.ML(   features_train = X_train,    task_type = "survival",   time_var = time_train,   event_var = event_train,   k_folds = 2,   n_rep = 1,   file_name = "Example_survival",   ncores = 1 ) names(res_survival$ML_Models) res_survival$Model$Model_object head(res_survival$Model$Prediction_folds)

title: pipeML
text: training, predictions can generated using compute_prediction(). Unlike classification models, survival models may return different types predictions depending model used. models predict risk score, others predict expected survival time survival probability. compute_prediction() function automatically handles differences. Internally, attempts several prediction types converts standardized risk score results can compared across models: Risk score (linear_pred) – typically produced Cox models. Higher values indicate higher predicted risk. Predicted survival time (time) – produced parametric survival models. Higher values indicate longer survival, values internally reversed represent risk. Survival probability (survival) – probability surviving given time point. Higher probabilities correspond lower risk, values also internally reversed. standardization step, predictions always interpreted way: Higher prediction values correspond higher predicted risk allows pipeML compute performance metrics concordance index (C-index) stratify patients risk groups Kaplan–Meier visualization. Figure 5. KM plot.
code: pred <- compute_prediction(   model = res_survival$Model,   test_data = X_test,   task_type = "survival",   time_var = time_test,   event_var = event_test,   file.name = "Example_survival")

title: pipeML
text: use function compute_shap_values computed time task_type = "survival".
code: shap_survival <- compute_shap_values(   model_trained = res_survival$Model,   data_train = df,   task_type = "survival",   time_col = "time",   event_col = "status",   n_cores = 2,   file.name = "Example_survival" )
